toc.title: Explanatory and reinforcing power of stories

blocks.p: Your autonomic nervous system moves among three basic states: [safety, flight/fight and shutdown](piece:autonomic-nervous-system). So, how does one access these states? What is the mechanism of action here?

Dr. Stephen Porges coined the term "neuroception" to describe the unconscious process of detecting cues of safety or danger from the external and internal environment. I've seen others call this the body's "threat detection system" or compare it to Spider-Man's superhuman Spider-Sense. These are helpful but incomplete. Neuroception does not detect only danger; it also detects safety.

External information from the environment passes through our five senses and then goes to very primitive parts of the brainstem outside of our conscious awareness. The brainstem makes the neuroceptive "decision" to shift autonomic state up or down the Polyvagal ladder. Ideally, the brainstem shifts to the appropriate ANS state and meets the needs of survival based on the context of the moment.

Neuroception has nothing to do with choice. It has everything to do with predetermined neurobiological responses to safety or danger. Evolution encoded these responses into DNA, generation after generation. The encoding helped our evolutionary ancestors survive long enough to pass on what helped them to autonomically survive to the next generation.

But neuroception also occurs internally; your body sends information to your brainstem, which receives this information and adjusts state. For example, if you are too hungry, you shift into a fight state and become hangry.

Each autonomic state restricts or enables the options of our different experiential domains: behaviors, sensations, impulses, emotions, and cognitions. In essence, the possibilities of these domains are controlled by each state. For example, the biology of the safety state unlocks access to the behaviors linked to social engagement, like gentle eye contact and a rich vocal range. You can't use these behaviors from flight/fight or shutdown (at least, not in a genuine social way).

As one's active state moves down the Polyvagal ladder, the individual loses access to the experiences higher up the ladder. When you enter the flight state, you lose the feelings of hope and joy that come from the safety state. When you enter shutdown, you lose the impulse to aggressively enforce boundaries that come from the fight state.

Imagine a wide-eyed young boy running from a dog. Is he capable of smiling and social engagement while fleeing? Of course not. Is it because he hasn't chosen to socially engage? No. Those behaviors are simply not accessible while in flight. He dropped down the Polyvagal ladder and is in a sympathetic survival mode. His body's potential is entirely skewed toward survival through mobilized evasion. His Polyvagal state (flight) dictates the limits of his experiences in behavior, cognitions, emotions, sensations, and impulses.

Even when in the same context, your state limits or expands your experience and behavior. If you're playing chess in your safety state, you'll be patient and think carefully. If you're playing chess from flight, you'll feel nervous and catastrophize a potential loss in your mind. If you're playing from shutdown... well, you may not have even shown up! You lack motivation to try since you'll lose anyway.

Shifts down the Polyvagal ladder are temporary. When the boy successfully escapes the dog and returns home, his ANS will return to its safety state. He'll go to his Mother and get a reassuring hug as she soothes him with her voice. He'll tell her the story, share a smile with her and perhaps even a laugh about the situation. He enters flight as he needs to, uses the mobilization, then returns to his safety state when in a safe environment and with a safe other. Although defensive states are temporary, it's possible to get stuck in them.
Some interpersonal cues are more predictable than others to provide a neuroception of safety or danger, though this varies across individuals.
Safety:

ul: use of facial muscles, especially the upper face

blocks.p: Danger:

ul: harsh tone of voice: too low or too high

blocks.p: We take in others' behaviors through our senses. These behaviors will trigger responses of safety or danger. When someone smiles genuinely, it triggers a neuroception of safety within us. When we see someone who has no facial movement, it triggers a neuroception of danger.

Other sensory inputs that don't involve people are also likely to trigger safety or danger as well. Environmental cues like the feel of a gentle breeze, the colors of a sunset, or the sound of waves crashing on the shore likely trigger safety. Other things will likely trigger defense, like loud, booming bass sounds or the prick of a thorn.

We don't choose how we feel about these, nor do we decide how we neurocept them. We simply take in the external stimuli through our senses. Then, that stimuli gets filtered through our brain stem, shifting our ANS state accordingly.

This discussion of the unconscious nature of neuroception may lead to a harsh, mechanical way to view ourselves. We're obviously not machines; we aren't computers running code. But, in a way, we kinda are. Humans can do incredible things that seem to detach us from the rest of the animal kingdom. We make tools that help us make other tools. We create incredible works of art and foods that seem to touch us to the core.

At the same time, underneath it all... we are very much biological organisms just like any other. Our bodies do indeed receive sensory inputs and shift state. I'm positive you can think of at least one example of your body doing something you didn't consciously want it to: a time when you froze when you would have preferred to fight; a time when you collapsed in helplessness when you really wanted to speak powerfully; a time when you desperately wanted to connect to someone but couldn't force yourself to hug them (or receive their hug).

While we are inherently biological organisms, we also seem to have a lot of choice every moment of every day. No, you can't choose to exist in your safety state in this moment. But, can you choose to extend your exhale? Can you choose to cut open a lime and mindfully smell it? Can you choose to step outside of your home and feel sunlight? It seems like we can generally choose within every small moment of the present. Those choices add up and help us access more safety. Yes, we're organisms and our state limits our experiences. But, we can influence our state to become more experientially expansive. As we access more safety, our neuroceptive triggers still exist, but we'll have more capacity to notice and use them in our decisions.

blocks.why: You can choose to feel sunlight or smell a lime. This practice gives your neuroception a cue of safety on purpose.

blocks.p: Let's do a quick experiment using your imagination. I'll share a story and you need to fill in the blanks. Notice what internal shifts are happening within you throughout the story. It may be difficult, but do the best you can to identify any small emotions or sensations from your body.

You're walking down a sidewalk after having gotten off of work. It's dark outside as you make your way to your car, about a block away. You can hear the dull hum of traffic in the distance. As you walk, you think about the day's events, particularly the stressful ones. You look down as you walk, remembering what someone said that upset you. (Pause here and recall something that recently upset you.) Your thoughts focus on the memory, wondering why that person talked to you that way, what you should have done differently, and so on. You feel . As you think, you lose connection with the sounds of the environment, including the footsteps from behind. When you do notice the footsteps, you feel . Your body feels the impulse to _.

You may have felt minor autonomic shifts within you as you imagined the scenario unfolding. You may have shifted into defensive activation accompanied by a slight impulse to run or use aggression on the potential danger. Or perhaps you tensed with a twist in your gut, feeling immobile with a tinge of fear.

You can notice neuroceptions as they happen or even afterward when thinking back. That's much more common; we look back and recognize these neuroceptive shifts in our autonomic state. After the fact, we can see when these shifts happened, identifying what state we were in and which we shifted to. We may also notice the environmental stimuli that triggered the state shift.

But commonly, we don't. What we neurocept as safe or dangerous easily goes unnoticed, even when we examine the situation later on. There could be otherwise benign aspects of the environment that mean something to a particular individual and they don't realize they are cues of danger.

I was working with a teen on identifying what fidget might help her to discharge some stuck defensive energy. I offered her a green rubber ring with spikes all around it. She declined with a forceful shake of her head but offered no explanation. She explained later in the session that the color green causes her to feel nauseous, green being the color of her Father's corpse the last time she saw him.

Green has no inherent meaning or value. It's just a color. It's probably more likely to be a neuroception of safety for most people due to the greens in nature. But for this person, the color green had meaning: not primarily a cognitive meaning but more a visceral one. She felt the bottom-up activation during the session, a defensive neuroception experienced as nausea.

Neuroception has some generally predictable elements. However, neuroceptive triggers and autonomic shifts vary from person to person. Traumatized individuals may show the greatest variance. You may have your own version of green, something that triggers defensive activation for you but no one else: a specific place, object, scent, sound, or texture.

"Healthy" neuroception means functional based on external and internal survival needs for the organism in the present moment. "Healthy" does not refer to "good." "Healthy" does not carry judgment either. "Healthy" refers to being biologically optimal to maintain ideal body functioning and respond to contextual danger. ("Functional neuroception" might be a better phrase.)

Through healthy neuroception, the body detects and shifts to the appropriate state based on contextual needs. The body uses social behavior in a safe environment with safe people, and it does not use defenses like fighting or fleeing unless it is in a dangerous environment.

The individual with healthy neuroception accurately detects safety cues and then climbs to the top of their Polyvagal ladder (or maintains access to it). This individual might be a student who goes to a safe school, lives in a safe home, and can sit in class, interact with others appropriately, and learn. The student neurocepts safety in their life contexts, and their behaviors follow.

This same student can also access their defensive states when necessary, like when actual environmental danger cues trigger defense. They will feel mobilization if they hear a loud, booming sound in the distance. At that moment, their body will access flight activation. If they cannot flee a dangerous situation, they will access fight. If they cannot escape or fight, they will neurocept life-threat and immobilize. This sequence is the path of healthy neuroception based on environmental cues. (Healthy neuroception also applies to accurately receiving cues of danger from the internal world, then shifting state appropriately based on context.)

Again, this is not an issue of the individual choosing to react or choosing to neurocept and shift state. Neuroception is an unconscious process that aided our evolutionary ancestors in surviving and passing on their genetic material without conscious direction or control. They needed to accurately and immediately detect safety and danger, shift state, and shift behaviors. These processes are still alive within us now.

Through "unhealthy" neuroception, the body does not accurately detect or shift state based on the environment. The body does not fight or flee when in a dangerous environment, and the body does not use social behavior in a safe environment. In other words, the individual's threat detector is missing threats, and their safety detector is missing safety. Or, if it's detecting, it's not shifting to the appropriate state.

Unhealthy neuroception may be why some traumatized individuals continually repeat the same harmful decisions and even why trauma passes from one generation to the next. They don't recognize danger in others and don't respond appropriately. They also don't recognize safety when it's there. They end up feeling "safe" with dangerous individuals and feel "danger" with safe individuals. They unknowingly fill their lives with the wrong people, repeating the same disastrous relationships.

The following is a common scenario of generational trauma I've seen in my practice: the Mom whom her authoritarian stepfather sexually abused doesn't pick up on the danger of her short-term boyfriend living with her and her own children. She feels a pseudo-connection to him and does not identify his red flags: he's jealous, controlling, and demanding. The short-term boyfriend sexually abuses a child in the home, and Mom denies it occurred when the child comes to her. This dynamic creates a new generation of sexual trauma by a substitute authoritarian Father.

The Mother's unhealthy neuroception thwarted her from detecting the boyfriend's danger cues early on. She did not neurocept other red flags that may have been occurring right under her nose, like inappropriate gift-giving from him to one child in particular. It also prevented her from listening to her children and taking them seriously. Instead of mobilizing with flight/fight energy to protect her children, she denies the allegation and retreats into pseudo-connection with her boyfriend.

As she looks back from her safety state, those red flags become more apparent, and she'll realize the cues that she saw but didn't register as dangerous. She may remember the first time the boyfriend erupted in anger over something minuscule. Or a "joke" he made with a perverse sexual innuendo that was far from appropriate. She can look back and see the escalation of control over her children and his manipulation of her emotions when the child raised the alarm and told the truth. At the moment, she missed these red flags because of an unhealthy neuroception from her traumatic past. Later, as she builds more safety in her system and can think clearly, these things will become painfully obvious.

I'm sure you see the child victim in this scenario may end up stuck in trauma and repeat this dysfunctional pattern. As an adolescent, the abused child will find comfort in romantic partners that soothe their emotions, providing a pseudo connection and a false sense of safety. The partner will use the adolescent for their own selfish motives, and the adolescent will miss the red flags, like forcing them to share their mobile location at all times. As the adolescent enters adulthood, the same patterns solidify. They will consistently seek connection with others and find it in the wrong people. Their unhealthy neuroception will keep them from using their flight and fight inner power, preventing them from forming real, safe, loving connections with trustworthy friends and partners.

I've worked with kids, adolescents, adults, and families and, sadly, have seen this scenario unfold many times. I've seen it at every stage through the various age groups I've worked with. Maybe not exactly like this, but some variation of this general story. Of course, this does not have to be a predetermined outcome for anyone, and steps can be taken to prevent this potential from becoming a reality. If you identify with this story (or your own version), I hope the Polyvagal Trauma Relief System assists you with stopping the generational cycle. Please seek out a professional to work with if needed.

Have you ever noticed that sometimes your thoughts are more hopeful, empathetic, or compassionate? And sometimes they're more anxious, aggressive, or sullen? Have you noticed your thoughts change depending on your feelings? When you're feeling positive, your thoughts are positive. When you're feeling negative, your thoughts are negative, right?

Our thoughts come from our Polyvagal state, just like behaviors, emotions, sensations, and impulses. Deb Dana aptly phrases it this way: "Story Follows State." Stories sound many different ways, like these:

ul: "I appreciate who and what I have in life."
"I'm never going to pass this test. I'll always be a failure."
"It's your fault I feel this way!"
"I'm so useless and unlovable. What's wrong with me?"

blocks.p: In our state of safety, our thoughts will be more empathetic, understanding, validating, and normalizing. In flight/fight, thoughts will be more anxious, catastrophizing, avoidant, or aggressive. And in shutdown, thoughts will be pessimistic, lacking hope or belief, and devoid of purpose.

blocks.h: Explanatory and reinforcing power of stories

blocks.p: Stories make sense of what caused an autonomic state shift, but are a reflection of one's current state. For example, when spouses argue, they often have the story, "It's your fault I feel this way." That story explains their state shift, but it's a reflection of their current state (probably fight). If they felt more positive (more safety), their story would change to something like, "I'm feeling some anger coming up. I'm stopping here, but will try again once I feel calmer."

However, our state's stories do not necessarily reflect reality. In essence, stories can be wrong. The thought, "What happened to me is my fault because of what I was wearing" is obviously incorrect. But the thought nevertheless provides an explanation.

The explanatory power of these stories also serve another function: to reduce the overwhelming nature of defensive activation. Stories act as containers. If one truly felt their inner state and its accompanying emotions, impulses, and sensations, it would likely be overwhelming. Those underlying experiences are intense if one is unprepared. Stories provide an explanation which contains the defensive activation.

Sadly, stories reduce defensive activation but also reinforce it. The thought, "It's my fault" reinforces the individual's defensive activation. This creates a self-reinforcing loop: the defensive state creates the incorrect cognition of self-blame. The self-blame reinforces the defensive state, which reinforces the self-blame. The individual is seemingly forever stuck in negative thinking and defensive activation.

Stories perhaps most noticeably occur regarding a traumatic incident or significant defensive state activation (like arguing with a spouse). However, we always create stories. Our underlying autonomic states consistently and directly influence our thoughts throughout a normal day. If your thoughts are often on the negative side, you're likely chronically in a defensive state. Your chronic defensive state perpetually feeds you negative thinking, like rumination and even obsessions.

Think back to my client's example of having a nauseous reaction to the green rubber fidget ring. Her body responded to the sight of the green rubber ring, feeling nauseous, something she said is common for her with green stimuli. Let's break down what happens within her from the perspective of the Polyvagal Theory.

When she sees the green ring, her state unconsciously shifts. She then consciously experiences nausea, then remembers the image of her deceased Father and thinks, "I don't like green." She didn't first see the green, then think, "I don't like green," then have a nauseous reaction. The story of not liking green followed the memory (another kind of "story" in this example: a visual one). These stories followed the biological autonomic shift, felt as nausea.

Her brain attempts to explain the state shift in response to the stimuli. "I felt shutdown, therefore I don't like green," says the brain. And that's both true and not true. Suppose we were to successfully renegotiate the trauma response for this client and get her more access to her safety state. In that case, she might discover she doesn't really have any aversion to the color green and maybe even likes it. But currently, she doesn't like green since she neurocepts it as life-threat, based on past circumstances.

Remember, stories can help explain but are also helpful in containing the state shift. The story "I don't like green" provides her with an avenue to get a sense of control over the state shift and possibly to avoid falling further down her Polyvagal ladder. Instead of actively remembering and thinking about the image of her Father, she can think, "I don't like green," and leave it at that. She can also avoid future trauma triggering by avoiding the color green.

However, the story also provides an avenue for her to communicate with me as a supportive person, which will also help her to maintain her spot on the ladder. Her noticing the "I don't like green" story is the first step toward getting to the next story, which is the memory of her deceased Father. This second story, the memory, is a direct visual connection to the experience of the state shift from the traumatic experience. If we simply stay with the "I don't like green" story, we'd be one step removed from the direct experience of the autonomic state, a state she went into in the past but is recurring in the present moment of the therapy session.
Here's what to take with you:

ul: Autonomic nervous system: our internal processes are on autopilot
Neuroception: our safety and threat detection system that shifts our autonomic state
Story follows state: our thoughts are a result of our state

blocks.prompt: Do you recognize any of your own stories? (yes or no)
Is it possible these are inaccurate attempts to explain some traumatizing event? (yes or no)
Is it possible the story helps contain some inner pain? (yes or no)
What other stories better explain the event based on your understanding of the Polyvagal Theory? (apply your knowledge so far)

blocks.p: If you want to journal or reflect on these more deeply, please do so. However, it may be best to keep it light and simple for now.

q: "Even though we may not be aware of danger on a cognitive level, on a neurophysiological level, our body has already started a sequence of neural processes that would facilitate adaptive defense behaviors..." (Porges)
blocks.cite: Porges, S. W. (2004). Neuroception. Zero to Three.

blocks.p: My translation: Our body is aware of danger before our thoughts are.

q: "Every single one of us contends with states of threat, which are our responses to the uncertainty of survival. Threat can emanate from the external world or arise internally from memories. I devised the term neuroception to describe how -below the level of conscious awareness- neural circuits constantly monitor and assess internal and external risks, whether situations or people, as safe, dangerous, or life-threatening." (Porges)
blocks.cite: Porges, S. W. (2021). The anatomy of calm. In “A sigh of relief.” Psychology Today, September/October 2021, 38–39.

blocks.p: My translation: Porges created the term, "neuroception" to describe our constant monitoring of risk from outside and inside our bodies. It's unconscious.

q: "...Neuroception is proposed as a 'reflexive' mechanism capable of instantaneously shifting physiological state. Neuroception is a plausible mechanism mediating both the expression and the disruption of positive social behavior, emotion regulation, and visceral homeostasis. Neuroception might be triggered by feature detectors involving areas of temporal cortex that communicate with the central nucleus of the amygdala and the periaqueductal gray, since limbic reactivity is modulated by temporal cortex responses to biological movements including voices, faces, and hand movements...." (Porges & Kolacz)
blocks.cite: Porges, S. W., & Kolacz, J. (2018). Neurocardiology through the lens of the polyvagal theory. In R. J. Gelpi & B. Buchholz (Eds.), Neurocardiology: Pathophysiological Aspects and Clinical Implications. Elsevier.

blocks.p: My translation: Neuroception instantly changes our body's state and affects social behavior, emotions, and internal balance. It might be triggered by brain areas that respond to voices, faces, and hand movements.
